outline.description: This chapter introduces the parties, the technological subject matter involving Passive Intermodulation (PIM) mitigation, and the procedural history leading to the Federal Circuit's review. It establishes the stakes of the litigation, including the massive damages award, and outlines the specific relief sought by the appellants (AT&T and Nokia) regarding Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL) and new trials.
subtopics: Parties and Technology: Finesse Wireless vs. AT&T/Nokia and PIM Cancellation Methods
Procedural Posture: Jury Verdict, Damages Award ($166M), and Denial of JMOL/New Trial
Standard of Review: De Novo JMOL Analysis under Fifth Circuit Law vs. Substantial Evidence Standard

outline.chapter_title: Infringement Analysis of the '134 Patent: The Failure of Expert Mapping
outline.description: This chapter provides a deep dive into the court's reversal regarding U.S. Patent No. 7,346,134. It focuses on Claim 1's requirement to sample both 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals.' The analysis centers on why Plaintiff's expert testimony failed to prove infringement due to internal contradictions regarding signal timing and identification.
subtopics: Claim Construction: Defining 'Signals of Interest' versus 'Interference Generating Signals'
The Timing Paradox: Why Modeled PIM Paths Cannot Be Sampled Before Generation
Expert Testimony Breakdown: Dr. Wells' Contradictory Identification of Red Path Signals (DL(TX) vs. Modeled PIM)
Application of Johns Hopkins Precedent: Why Conflicting Expert Opinions Cannot Support a Verdict

outline.chapter_title: Infringement Analysis of the '775 Patent: Multiplication Requirements and Prosecution History Estoppel
outline.description: This chapter examines U.S. Patent No. 9,548,775, addressing two critical issues: whether amending claims to specify 'three signals' surrendered scope for devices using only two unique signals, and whether the accused device performed the specific seven mathematical multiplications required by the claim. It clarifies why prosecution history arguments were rejected but factual evidence failures led to reversal.
subtopics: Prosecution History Estoppel Argument: Did Amending to 'Three Signals' Surrender Two-Signal Scope?
Rejection of Estoppel: Distinction Between Overcoming Active IMP Prior Art vs. Disavowing Unique Signal Counts
The Seven-Multiplication Limitation: Requirement for Specific Mathematical Operations (S1 x S1 x S2, etc.)
Insufficiency of Evidence: Mismatch Between Accused Device Operations (Modulus/Conjugates) and Claimed Multiplications

outline.description: This final chapter explains the logical consequence of reversing the infringement findings on all counts. It details why a separate analysis of damages was rendered moot once non-infringement was established via JMOL, resulting in the vacation of the $166 million award.
subtopics: Relationship Between Infringement Findings and Dam Awards
